titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §258–277: herdsmen, wages and hire-rates (xxxviii 5 – xxxix 57)
part: Laws §258–277 · herdsmen, wages & hire-rates (Col. xxxviii 5 – xxxix 57)
about: Twenty laws on the rates for hired work and on what a hired herdsman owes. First the yearly wages in grain: six kor for a ŠÀ.GUD, a worker whose title I cannot read and who may have to do with oxen (§258), and eight kor for a herdsman of cattle and sheep (§261), with fines for stealing a plough or one of two other farm implements whose names I cannot read (§259–260). §262 breaks off after a few words, and the next six lines of the column (xxxviii 31–36) are not preserved in Harper’s edition, so there is a gap. Then the herdsman’s duties (§263–267): he replaces an ox with an ox and a sheep with a sheep if he has lost them; if he has been paid and is content and still diminishes the herd, he pays the young and the yield by his contract; if he cheats and sells animals he is convicted and replaces tenfold; if a plague or a lion strikes the pen he clears himself before the god and the owner bears the loss; if he is careless he makes the damage good. The rest are day-rates: hired animals for threshing (§268–270), cattle with wagon and driver or the wagon alone (§271–272), a hired worker, dearer in the first half of the year (§273), skilled craftsmen by trade (§274, a list that is broken in the middle), and boats (§275–277). Several words are not readable from the grammar and I say so in the notes: ŠÀ.GUD, the two tools of §260, kazzatum and ḫiditum, lalâm, maḫirtum, most of the trade names of §274 and some verbs (uṣṣaḫḫir, ubbamma). Col. XXXVIII ends at line 101 and col. XXXIX is followed to line 57; Harper’s line numerals agree with his section headings throughout.

sentences.i: If a man has hired an ox-driver (?),
sentences.n: This part (§258–277) is the code’s tariff of hire for herdsmen, ploughmen, draught animals, threshers, wagons, hired workers and boats; most of the laws are one short condition and one price. They open with the usual šumma pattern: šumma awīlum … īgur “if a man has hired …”. īgur is the preterite of agārum “to hire”, here meaning “has hired” (as in §242). The man hired is written ŠÀ.GUD, two signs, a Sumerogram (a word written in Sumerian signs) that I cannot read in Akkadian; that he is some worker with oxen (an ox-driver, perhaps a ploughman) is only my guess, from the GUD “ox” inside the word and from §259, where a plough follows. So the word is left unread and marked uncertain.

sentences.i: he shall give him six kor of grain a year.
sentences.n: The price. 6 is the one sign for six; ŠE.GUR is two signs, “grain” and “kor” (the large measure of capacity, about 300 litres), written as Sumerograms with no ending; I say it kur šeʾam “a kor of grain”, with the number before it in the form that goes with a masculine noun (šeššet; reconstructed spoken form (?)). ina šattim 1 is “in the year, one”: MU (“year”) with no ending, then the numeral 1 and the sign KAM, which is silent after a numeral. inaddiššum is inaddin, the present of nadānum “to give”, plus -šum “to him”, with the final n of inaddin assimilated to the š of the suffix: “he shall give him”. As everywhere in the code, the present tense of the penalty means “shall”.

sentences.i: If a man has stolen a plough in the field,
sentences.n: GIŠ.APIN is two Sumerograms, GIŠ “wood” and APIN, the sign Harper’s List of Signs gives for the plough (epinnum); I say it epinnam (reconstructed spoken form (?)). ugarim is the field or meadow (ugārum; Harper’s glossary: “field, meadow”); on the plate it is the Sumerogram A.GÀR, two signs, with no ending written. iš-ri-iq is išriq, the preterite of šarāqum “to steal”, so “he stole” (the perfect ištariq, “has stolen”, follows in §260).

sentences.l: five shekels of-silver to-the-owner of-the-plough he-shall-give.
sentences.i: he shall pay five shekels of silver to the owner of the plough.
sentences.n: V GÍN KÙ.BABBAR: the numeral 5 (one sign), GÍN “shekel” and KÙ.BABBAR “silver”, each a Sumerogram with no ending, said ḫamšat šiqil kaspim “five shekels of silver” (the number is a reconstructed spoken form (?)). ana bēl epinnim, “to the owner of the plough”: bēl is bēlum “lord, owner” (BE + EL), in the construct before the noun it owns. The thief pays the owner five shekels: this is a fixed fine, not the return of the plough.

sentences.i: If he has stolen a GIŠ.APIN.TUK.KIN or a GIŠ.GAN.UR (two farm implements; unread),
sentences.n: No subject is written (šumma has no awīlum after it), so “he” means anyone. The two things stolen are Sumerograms I cannot read: GIŠ.APIN.TUK.KIN (wood-sign, plough-sign, TUK, KIN; Harper’s sign list gives the whole string as one entry under GIŠ) and GIŠ.GAN.UR (wood-sign, GAN, UR). They are plainly tools of the plough-team, since the penalty is three shekels, lower than for the plough itself, but what they are I do not know, and I do not translate them. I key the GAN sign as the plain gan sign (an uncertain identification) and the UR as the dog-sign. u lu is “or”: two words written together, ù “and” (the sign Ù) + lu “or” (the sign LU), as in §241–257. ištariq is the perfect of šarāqum, “has stolen”.

sentences.i: he shall pay three shekels of silver.
sentences.n: The fine is three shekels (III GÍN KÙ.BABBAR; I say šalāšat šiqil kaspim, with the number as a reconstructed spoken form (?), the feminine form before the masculine šiqil, as in §241–257). The law does not say who receives it; §259 names the owner, and the same is surely meant.

sentences.l: If a-man a-herdsman for-cattle and-sheep to-pasture has-hired,
sentences.i: If a man has hired a herdsman to pasture cattle and sheep,
sentences.n: The herdsman is written NA.KAD, two Sumerograms (Harper’s glossary gives nāqidum “herdsman” as NA.KAD; on the plate there are two signs, and I say nāqidam). The KAD sign is only tentatively identified. LID.GUD.ZUN is “cattle” (liātum, a collective, the cows), a four-part Sumerogram (ÁB, GU₄, ḪI, A) whose last two signs are the plural marker; U₈.UDU{ḫi.a} is “sheep and goats” (ṣēnum), also with the plural marker. The marker is silent when read aloud. u is the conjunction “and” (the plate sign U₃). ri-im is written as Harper has it, and I take it for the infinitive of rêʾûm “to pasture”: ana rēʾîm “to pasture” (the spelling is odd, so UNCERTAIN). īgur “has hired”.

sentences.i: he shall give him eight kor of grain a year.
sentences.n: The same wage formula as §258, with VIII ŠE.GUR: eight kor of grain a year. 8 is one sign (the numeral eight), said samānat (reconstructed (?)).

sentences.i: If a man … an ox or a sheep
sentences.n: §262 is broken. Harper prints only its opening, šumma awīlum alpam ù lu immeram “if a man … an ox or a sheep”, and the rest of this law is in the lacuna that follows (the next unit). The verb and the penalty are lost; I do not guess them. alpam is the one sign GU₄ “ox”, with no -am written (the plate has four signs on this line after šumma awīlum: GU₄, Ù, LU, UDU); ù lu is “or”, two words (as in §260); immeram is the one sign UDU (the LU sign) “sheep”, with no -am written.

sentences.i: to … (the rest of the law is lost)
sentences.n: A gap. This is where §262 breaks off: a-na “to”, then a row of damage on the plate (Harper draws the stele’s hatched, broken surface after the second sign). Harper’s transliteration then prints nothing for lines 31–36 either: the stele is lost for six more lines, so §262 is incomplete, and the next law that survives is §263, which starts on line 37. These lines are shown as one gap; nothing is reconstructed. The loss is on the stele itself, not in this edition.

sentences.l: If [an-ox] or a-sheep which was-given-to-him he-has-destroyed,
sentences.i: If he has lost the [ox] or sheep that was given to him,
sentences.n: The square brackets are Harper’s: [alpam] “an ox” is restored from the parallel in the next lines, where the plate’s outline signs mark the parts of the stone that are damaged. ša innadnušum “which was given to him” is the passive of nadānum (the N-stem, with the n assimilated: innadnušum, the -šum “to him” attached). uḫtalliq is the D-stem perfect of ḫalāqum “to perish”, in D “to make perish, to destroy” (the same verb as in §232 ff.; said of animals entrusted to him, “lost”): the owner’s animal, entrusted to the herdsman, is lost through him. The animal words carry no -am: GU₄ (restored) and UDU stand alone, as on line 29, and ù lu is “or”, two words.

sentences.l: an-ox in-place-of [an-ox], a-sheep in-place-of [a-sheep], to their-owners he-shall-replace.
sentences.i: he shall replace ox for ox and sheep for sheep to their owners.
sentences.n: alpam kīma [alpim] “an ox like an ox”, immeram kīma [immerim] “a sheep like a sheep”: kīma “like, in place of” (KI + MA). The brackets are Harper’s restorations of the second word of each pair. On the plate each of the two lines begins with the animal sign alone (GU₄ on line 40, the sheep sign UDU on line 41, no -am written), then the diamond-shaped KI and the long horizontal MA, then, in outline, the restored second animal sign. iriab is the present of riābum “to replace” (as in §245): “he shall replace”. bēlīšunu is “their owners” (bēlum + -šunu).

sentences.l: If a-herdsman to-whom cattle or sheep to-pasture were-given,
sentences.i: If a herdsman to whom cattle or sheep have been given to pasture
sentences.n: A long law, in four units. This first one is the protasis (the “if” part): šumma rēʾûm ša liātim ù lu ṣēnī ana rēʾîm innadnušum, literally “if a herdsman, who cattle or sheep for pasturing were-given-to-him”. rēʾûm “herdsman, shepherd” is the Sumerogram SIPA, written PA + LU (the brackets mark Harper’s restoration of the damaged word). ša is the relative “who, to whom”; the clause ends in the passive innadnušum “was/were given to him” (see §263). ana rēʾîm “for pasturing” as in §261.

sentences.i: has received his wage … (a damaged phrase), and is satisfied,
sentences.n: Two short clauses. Á-šu is idīšu “his wage” (Á is the Sumerogram for idum “hire, wage”, and -šu “his”); maḫir is the stative of maḫārum “to receive”, “he has received”. libbašu ṭāb is literally “his heart is good”, an idiom for “he is content, satisfied”. The middle of line 49 is damaged on the plate: Harper reads mimma(?) “whatever, anything” in the broken stretch (shown here as a gap) and ḫar(?)-ra-tim after it, both with a query of his own; I do not know the word ḫarratim, so the stretch between “his wage” and “has received” is left untranslated. The sense of the whole is plain from the next words: the herdsman has been paid and has no complaint.

sentences.i: has made the cattle fewer and the sheep fewer,
sentences.n: uzzaḫḫir is Harper’s reading uz-za-aḫ-ḫi-ir (with the first sign in brackets, restored): I take it for the D-stem of ṣeḫērum “to be small”, so “has made small, has diminished, reduced”, said uṣṣaḫḫir (Harper’s glossary lists it as an intransitive stem, “to be diminished”, which would make the cattle themselves the subject). This is UNCERTAIN: the form fits a D-stem only loosely, and the two readings differ in who does the diminishing. Harper prints the first word as LID.GUN.ZUN (GUN, not GUD as in every other place); I read the usual LID.GUD.ZUN “cattle” (the plate sign is the same as the GUD of line 45) and take Harper’s GUN for a misprint (the sign GUN means “yield”, and nothing here calls for it).

sentences.l: the-offspring he-has-reduced, according-to the-terms of-his-contract the-offspring and the-yield he-shall-give.
sentences.i: has reduced the young, he shall give the young and the yield according to the terms of his contract.
sentences.n: talittam is “the young (of the herd), the offspring” (talittum, from a root meaning “to bear”); umtaṭṭi is the D-stem perfect of maṭûm “to be few”, so “has reduced” (Harper’s um-ta-di; the sign di here stands for ṭi). ana pî riksātīšu is “according to the mouth of his contracts”: KA (mouth) is the Sumerogram for pûm “mouth, wording”, so ana pî means “according to the words of, as stated in”; riksātīšu is “his bindings, the terms of his contract” (riksum). The apodosis (the “then” part): talittam u biltam inaddin “he shall give the young and the yield”, i.e. what the herd should have produced (biltum is the yield, as in §26–41). The house rendering of ana pî ṣimdat šarrim (“according to the king’s schedule”) shows the same construction.

sentences.l: If a-herdsman to-whom cattle and sheep to-pasture were-given,
sentences.i: If a herdsman to whom cattle and sheep have been given to pasture
sentences.n: The same opening as §264, now with u (“and”) between cattle and sheep rather than ù lu (“or”), and with no break in the line. A herdsman who cheats with the herd he has been given: the verbs follow.

sentences.l: has-been-dishonest and the-mark has-changed and for-silver has-given,
sentences.i: has been dishonest (?), has changed the mark (?) and has sold them for silver,
sentences.n: Three verbs joined by -ma and u: a D-stem preterite (uṣarrirma), a D-stem perfect (uttakkir) and a perfect (ittadin). uṣarrirma (u-ṣa-ar-ri-ir-ma; Harper prints a dot under the a of ṣa, plainly a misplaced dot) is the D-stem of ṣarārum, which I take to mean “to be false, to cheat” (Harper’s glossary: ṣarāru II “to be dishonest”); the sense “has been dishonest” is UNCERTAIN (a D-stem “to falsify”). šimtam: Harper’s glossary gives šimtu as “destiny, contract, decisions, fate”, none of which suits the sale of animals, so I guess “mark, brand” (the owner’s mark on his animals, which a thief would alter before selling) from the context alone: UNCERTAIN; uttakkir is the D-stem perfect of nakārum “to be foreign, to alter”, so “has changed (the mark)”. ana kaspim ittadin is “has given for silver”, the commonest way to say “has sold” (as in §39–41).

sentences.l: they-shall-convict-him, and up-to tenfold of-what he-stole the-cattle and the-sheep to their-owners he-shall-replace.
sentences.i: they shall convict him, and he shall replace the cattle and sheep to their owners, up to ten times what he stole.
sentences.n: ukannūšuma is “they shall convict him, and” (kânum, D-stem: “to prove (guilty)”; -šu “him”, -ma “and”; as in §185–194). The penalty: adu ešrīšu ša išriqu is literally “up to his tenfold of what he stole”: a-du is “up to” (a variant of adi, as in earlier parts), 10-šu “its tenfold”, ša išriqu “which he stole” (išriq plus the ending -u that marks a clause after ša, the preterite of šarāqum as in §259). Harper prints the numeral here as X (the sign for 10). The object follows: cattle and sheep (LID.GUD.ZUN, u, U₈.UDU), to their owners (ana bēlīšunu), iriab “he shall replace” (riābum, as in §263).

sentences.l: If in-the-pen a-stroke of-the-god has-happened, or a-lion has-killed, the-herdsman before-the-god
sentences.i: If a plague (?) (lit. a stroke of the god) has broken out in the pen, or a lion has killed (animals), the herdsman
sentences.n: This law sets the herdsman’s duty when the herd is lost through no fault of his. tarbaṣim is the animal-pen or fold, written out syllabically, tar-ba-ṣi-im (Harper’s glossary: tarbaṣum “stable, fold”). lipit ilim is “a stroke of the god” (Harper’s glossary: liptu “stroke, visitation”, from lapātum “to touch”, so literally a touch), which I take to mean “plague, epidemic”; ittabši is “has occurred, has happened” (the perfect of bašûm, as in §112–126). I give “plague” with the literal sense beside it and mark it uncertain. UR.MAḪ is “lion” (house reading nēšum, §244); iddūk is the perfect of dâkum “to kill” (id-du-uk, with the doubled d, as in §244), here “has killed” (no object is written). Line 78 holds both the end of this condition and the start of the main clause, rēʾûm maḫar ilim, “the herdsman, before the god”: the herdsman is the subject of the oath-clearing in the next unit.

sentences.l: he-shall-clear-himself, and the-loss of-the-pen the-owner of-the-pen shall-accept from-him.
sentences.i: he shall clear himself, and the owner of the pen shall accept the loss of the pen from him.
sentences.n: ubbamma, “he shall clear himself, and”, is read from the grammar: -ma “and” on a form of the D-stem of ebēbum “to be clean” (D “to clear, purify”); the spelling u-ub-ba-am is not a form I can make fit fully, so the sense is UNCERTAIN. Taking an oath of purification “before the god” (maḫar ilim) is how a herdsman showed he was not at fault. miqitti tarbaṣim is “the falling (loss) of the pen”, the loss that happened in the pen (miqittum, from maqātum “to fall”; Harper’s glossary: “a fall, disaster”; the sign after mi is KI, read qi₂). bēl tarbaṣim imaḫḫaršu is “the owner of the pen shall receive (it) from him” (maḫārum “to receive”, present, + -šu): the owner has to accept the loss and cannot demand the animals back from the herdsman. imaḫḫaršu is uncertain in its -šu (“from him”).

sentences.l: If a-herdsman was-careless-and in-the-pen a-kazzatum has-caused, the-herdsman the-loss of-the-kazzatum which in-the-pen he-caused
sentences.i: If a herdsman was careless and has brought about a harm (?) in the pen, the herdsman — the loss (?) of the harm that he brought about in the pen —
sentences.n: i-gu-ma is igûma “he was careless, and” (egûm “to be careless”, spelled as in §112–126; Harper’s glossary has the same verb). The harm is kazzatum, a word I cannot read exactly: Harper’s glossary glosses it “injury”, and I follow that with the query. kaz is not a single sign I can find in the list; I write it as the two signs ka + az, which is UNCERTAIN. uštabši is the Š-perfect of bašûm, “has caused to be, has brought about” (house reading, as in §112–126); ušabšû is its preterite with the ending -u, “which he caused to be”. ḫidit kazzatim is “the loss (?) of the harm”: ḫiditum is read as “loss, damage” (Harper’s glossary: “blame, reproach, disaster, loss”), UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: the-cattle and the-sheep he-shall-make-good, to their-owners he-shall-give.
sentences.i: he shall make good the cattle and sheep, and give them to their owners.
sentences.n: ušallamma is “he shall make whole, he shall make good, and” (šalāmum, D-stem, as in §112–126; -ma “and” between the two verbs). The things he makes good are LID.GUD.ZUN u ṣēnī, “cattle and sheep”. Harper prints GUN for GUD in the first word here too (see §264). inaddin “he shall give”.

sentences.l: If a-man an-ox for-threshing has-hired, 20 qa of-grain its-hire.
sentences.i: If a man has hired an ox for threshing, its hire is 20 qa of grain.
sentences.n: Three parallel laws, one animal each (ox, donkey, a third animal), all for threshing (dīāšum, from the verb dâšum “to thresh”; ana dīāšim “for threshing”), each with a fixed hire. 20 is the sign U U (two tens); SÌLA is qa (about a litre) and the grain follows as ŠE with no ending: “twenty qa of grain”; Á-šu is idīšu “his (its) hire”, a bare noun-phrase with no verb, “its hire (is) …”. No time is given here; §271–272 give rates per day, so a day may be meant, but that is not written.

sentences.l: If a-donkey for-threshing he-has-hired, 10 qa of-grain its-hire.
sentences.i: If he has hired a donkey for threshing, its hire is 10 qa of grain.
sentences.n: As §268, with ANŠE “donkey” (imēram; the plate shows the single sign, as at §241–257) and the hire halved to 10 qa (the numeral is the single sign U, spoken ešret (?)). No awīlum follows šumma: “he” is anyone.

sentences.l: If a-lalâm for-threshing he-has-hired, 1 qa of-grain its-hire.
sentences.i: If he has hired a lalâm (a small animal?) for threshing, its hire is 1 qa of grain.
sentences.n: As §268–269, the hire here only one qa. The animal is the word Harper normalizes as lalâm; I do not know it (Harper’s glossary: “small animal, goat (?)”). The plate row shows two signs after šumma, which I read as LÁ + AM, and the word, from the price, must be a small animal (a kid or lamb?); it is UNCERTAIN and I leave it as lalâm. 1 is the single wedge, said ištēn (the form with a masculine noun, a reconstructed spoken form (?)).

sentences.l: If a-man cattle, a-wagon and its-driver has-hired,
sentences.i: If a man has hired cattle, a wagon and its driver,
sentences.n: Wagons. ṣumbam is “a wagon”, Harper’s glossary writing it GIŠ.MAR.GÍD.DA, four signs (wood, MAR, GÍD, DA); the second sign is MAR and the third is the sign I key as LAL (which also reads gíd), so the identification of GÍD is UNCERTAIN. murteddīša is “its driver” (murteddûm “one who leads on”, from redûm “to lead, drive”, with -ša “its”). The line break splits mu-ur-te-di-ša across a tier on the plate, as Harper marks, but it is one word. All three things are hired together, with the driver, by one hirer.

sentences.i: he shall pay 180 qa of grain a day.
sentences.n: ina ūmim 1 is “per day, one”: UD “day”, then the numeral 1 and the silent KAM (as ina šattim 1 for “a year”). The rate: CLXXX qa, written 𒐗 (the sign for three sixties, “180”; said šalāš šūšī, reconstructed (?)) with SÌLA qa and ŠE grain. For the cattle, wagon and driver together, 180 qa a day, i.e. 3 times 60.

sentences.l: If a-man the-wagon alone for-itself has-hired,
sentences.i: If a man has hired only the wagon, by itself,
sentences.n: ṣumbam-ma: the wagon with the emphasizing -ma, “the wagon only, the wagon alone”. ana ramānīša is literally “for her self”, “by herself, on her own” (ramānum “self”, -ša “her”: the wagon). So the hirer takes the wagon without the cattle or the driver; he supplies his own. Harper prints ṣumba-ma; I give the word the same signs as §271 and the ending -ma.

sentences.i: he shall pay 40 qa of grain a day.
sentences.n: The rate for the wagon alone: XL qa, 𒐏 the sign for four tens (spoken erbâ, reconstructed (?)), far below the 180 for team and driver together. Formula as §271.

sentences.i: If a man has hired a hireling,
sentences.n: Wages for a hired worker (agrum, the sign NAGAR with the person-marker {lú}, which is silent: as §26–41). The rate changes with the season, so the law is in two halves. īgur “has hired”.

sentences.l: from the-start of-the-year until the-fifth month, 6 grains of-silver per-day he-shall-give.
sentences.i: from the beginning of the year to the fifth month he shall pay six grains of silver a day.
sentences.n: ištu rēš šattim adi ḫamšim warḫim: “from the head of the year until the fifth month”. rēš is rēšum “head, beginning” (ri-eš); šattim is spelled out here, ša-at-tim, where elsewhere it was the one sign MU; ḫamšim is the ordinal “fifth” and ITI is warḫum “month” (the month-sign). The price is 6 ŠE: ŠE is the grain, here as a unit of weight for silver (a še is a “grain”, the smallest weight of silver, 1/180 of a shekel), so “six grains of silver”; the number is a reconstructed spoken form (?). inaddin “he shall give” closes the half.

sentences.l: from the-sixth month until the-… of-the-year, 5 grains of-silver per-day he-shall-give.
sentences.i: from the sixth month to the end (?) of the year he shall pay five grains of silver a day.
sentences.n: The second half, with the lower rate: ištu šeššim warḫim “from the sixth month” (ši-ši-im, the ordinal “sixth”, šeššum) adi taktida šattim “until the … of the year”. ta-ak-ti-da is a word I cannot place by form; Harper’s glossary lists taktida as “end” (no root given), which suits the sense, since the first half runs from the start of the year to the fifth month and this one from the sixth, but the word itself is UNCERTAIN. The rate is one grain lower, 5 ŠE a day (ḫamšat, reconstructed (?)).

sentences.i: If a man hires a craftsman,
sentences.n: A list of daily wages for skilled workers (mār ummiānim, literally “a son of a craftsman”, as in §185–194; DUMU “son” and UM.MI.A, three signs). iggar (i-ig-ga-ar) is a present of agārum “to hire” (Harper lists it under the same verb): here the present, not the preterite īgur of the other laws; I do not know why this law changes the tense. The list that follows is a series of short nominal clauses: idi X “the hire of an X”, then the price, with a single final clause for all of them: ina ūmim 1 inaddin “per day he shall pay”. Many of the trades are written with Sumerograms I cannot read, and the list is broken in the middle of the stone (the plate is hatched and the signs drawn in outline); where the signs are gone I show a gap.

sentences.i: The hire of a … (the trade is lost): 5 grains of silver.
sentences.n: Á is idum “hire”, in the construct before the worker’s name: idi “the hire of”. The trade’s name is lost in the damage (five dots in Harper, the hatched stone on the plate), after the man-sign {lú}, which is silent. 5 ŠE KÙ.BABBAR is “five grains of silver”.

sentences.i: The hire of a GAB.A (a trade; unread): 5 grains of silver.
sentences.n: The craft is written GAB.A with the man-sign {lú} before it; I cannot read it as an Akkadian word and leave it unread. The sign GAB is the breast-sign GABA (value gab); the A after it is the plain sign A. Harper prints the determinative here with an acute accent ({ámêlu}), which I take for a slip. UNCERTAIN.

sentences.i: The hire of a KAD (a trade; unread): 5 grains of silver.
sentences.n: The first sign of the line, Á “hire”, is restored by Harper (brackets) in the damaged stone; so is the numeral V and the ŠE sign’s beginning, [V ŠE]. The trade is written KAD, which I do not read; the sign is Harper’s no. 27 and its identification is TENTATIVE (the same sign is the second of NA.KAD “herdsman” in §261).

sentences.i: The hire of a GUL (a trade; unread): … grains of silver.
sentences.n: The trade is written GUL, with {lú}; unread. The number of grains is lost (the line begins in damage; Harper’s dots), only [ŠE] “grains” and KÙ.BABBAR “silver” remain, and ŠE is itself restored.

sentences.i: The hire of a GA(?) (a trade; unread): … grains of silver.
sentences.n: Harper prints GA with a query (raised “(?)”) after the {lú} sign: the sign is damaged and its reading is doubtful, so the trade is unread. The number is lost, as in the previous law.

sentences.i: The hire of a … (trade lost): … grains of silver.
sentences.n: Only the ending of the trade’s name survives, a sign Harper reads tu with a query. I show it as part of a gap with the final sign, and leave the trade unread. The number of grains is lost.

sentences.i: The hire of a … carpenter: 4 grains of silver.
sentences.n: The first part of the trade’s name is lost, but the word that remains is the carpenter, written with the single sign NAGAR (Harper normalizes it nangarim; the earlier part reads the same sign as agrum “hired man” in the {lú}-form, the glossary gives both agru and nangaru for it). The man-sign before it is in the damage. IV, 4, is the single sign for four (erbet, reconstructed (?)).

sentences.i: The hire of a SA (a trade; unread): 4 (?) grains of silver.
sentences.n: The trade is the single sign SA, which I do not read as a word (Harper’s own transliteration is the bare SA). The wage is four grains, one fewer than the earlier trades, as with the carpenter. On the plate the numeral of line 38 is lost in hatched surface (only ŠE, KÙ and BABBAR are drawn); Harper prints IV without brackets, which I take to be supplied from the carpenter’s line 36, so it is bracketed here and UNCERTAIN.

sentences.i: The hire of an AT.KIT (a trade; unread): … grains of silver.
sentences.n: AT.KIT is two Sumerograms, the signs AD and KID (kid, kit), which I cannot read as a word. The number is lost: Harper’s “. . : ŠE” leaves two dots and a colon-like mark in the break (the colon may be a damaged numeral), which I show as a gap.

sentences.i: The hire of a builder: … grains of silver.
sentences.n: ŠITIM is the Sumerogram for the builder, bānûm (as §228–233; the {lú} before it is silent). The number of grains is lost in the damage.

sentences.i: he shall pay that per day.
sentences.n: The one verb that governs the whole list of hires above: ina ūmim 1 inaddin “per day he shall pay”, each trade at its own rate. Harper restores [ūmi] and the first part of inaddin in the damage (brackets).

sentences.l: [If] a-man a-… -da(?) has-hired, per-day 3 grains of-silver is-her-hire.
sentences.i: If a man has hired a … (lost), her hire is 3 grains of silver per day.
sentences.n: Boats and their hire, in three short laws (§275–277). §275 is broken: the word hired is lost but for its last sign, which Harper reads da with a query; -ša “her” on idīša shows that it is a feminine thing. I take that to be a boat, since §276 and §277 are boat laws, but this law does not say so. The hire per day is 3 ŠE; Á-ša is idīša “her hire”, the hire of the thing, said of what is hired.

sentences.l: If a-maḫirtu he-has-hired, 2½ grains of-silver is-her-hire, per-day he-shall-give.
sentences.i: If he has hired a maḫirtu (a kind of boat?; unread), her hire is 2½ grains of silver, and he shall pay it per day.
sentences.n: maḫirtum is the word met in §234–239 (elippum ša maḫirtim “a boat of the maḫirtum”): a kind of boat whose sense is unknown, left untranslated and marked UNCERTAIN (the hire here, like §275 and §277, is a boat’s, which is why I take it for a boat). No man is named as hirer: “he”. The price is II½ ŠE: the numeral 2 and the half-sign (𒈦, the same sign as maš) one after the other, said šinā u mišil “two and a half” (reconstructed spoken form (?)).

sentences.l: If a-man a-boat of-60 kor has-hired,
sentences.i: If a man has hired a boat of 60 kor,
sentences.n: elippi, “of a boat”, is GIŠ.MÁ, two signs (wood and boat; as §215–240); LX GUR is “60 kor” (GEŠ₂, the sign for 60, then GUR “kor”): the boat’s size, as a load of 60 kor of grain. īgur “has hired”.

sentences.i: her hire is a sixth (of a shekel) of silver per day; he shall pay it.
sentences.n: ina ūmim 1 “per day” (UD, the numeral 1 and the silent KAM, as in §271) belongs here, with the price of the hire. IGI.VI.GAL is “a sixth”, šuššat: IGI, the numeral 6 and GAL, the Sumerogram written for a fraction; no word for “shekel” follows, but it is the shekel that is meant (as in the “quarter” of §225). KÙ.BABBAR “silver”; Á-ša idīša “her hire”; inaddin “he shall pay”.
